summary: Valid from, valid to: read a document as it stood, or as it will stand, on a date
detail: Carried forward from Genoa (2013, ~/Workshop/archive/post-peleton/Genoa/src/genoa/core/valid_from_valid_to.py), where hedge-fund use needed 'what did we believe on the 3rd'. Genoa's shape: an update closes the current row (valid_to = now) and inserts a new one under the same `ref`; `valid_on(date)` filters any query; many-to-many relations carry their own valid range; `find_or_create` on a date respects a version already dated in the future. Two kinds of time are involved, and eta has only one. Transaction time (when a write was recorded) is the ledger's -- delta's `delta_ledger`: ops, inverse and `at` per entry, so a document registered with the ledger can already be walked back to any moment, but only while the recorded paths still mean what they meant before the schema changed. Valid time (when something is true in the world: a price effective from Monday, a deal term that changes next quarter) is what Genoa's valid_from/valid_to gave and the ledger cannot, because it is written now about later. Design questions: (a) derive as-at reads from the ledger, with no schema change, or (b) put valid_from/valid_to on the tables and give a document's read() an `at`, or both, one for each kind of time; (c) name it as delta did, with the date in the document's name (`venue-at:42:2026-06-16`), so an as-at document is read-only and seen like any other; (d) how undo treats a future-dated write. Start with a story, per CLAUDE.md, not a feature: stories.md's Open 'Time' (the wedding's deadline, a story with a `when`) is where it meets the harness.
note: 2026-09-24: added after comparing eta with Genoa/Landfall (~/Workshop/archive/post-peleton/overview.md). Open, for Peter.

summary: Auto-UI for documents: a page drawn from a document's shape, with named components to override it
detail: The second thing carried forward from Genoa/Landfall (~/Workshop/archive/post-peleton/overview.md), and the thread the line has kept picking up. Landfall (2013): Genoa's describe_model() published every model's properties and types; `{label, model}` in ui.js gave a working list/view/edit panel; each value's template was looked up by `<mode>-<type>` (viewcell, editcell, inlinecell, viewfield, editfield), last registered wins, so one override changed every Image column; the settings, then a custom `js` panel, went further. It is what let Betts and Gilbert build fund screens without the architect, and most of Gilbert's 102 commits went into those generic screens. Since then: zeta DEC-10 (13 Sep 2026) derived a screen from a TypeScript `Table` that a test checks against the live schema (`zeta/describe.ts` is Genoa's describe.py again), with few rules in `zeta/derive.ts` and anything beyond them a hand-written node; apples' panel: every row has one, derived from the declaration, the same panel from every reading; hjeli's derive-ux in an earlier app. eta has the pieces but no derivation: bento's boxPage/collectionPage, `choice`, `row`, `cell`; applets registered by name (`registerApplet`, last wins, the same mechanism as data-micro) but placed by hand in each view (the wedding's picture-field is Landfall's editfield-image again). The tension is with eta's own rules: 'Build nothing no story needs', 'Not generated code', and the 17 Sep review's YAGNI D. So derive at render time, never generate files; derive from the document (what read() returns, or a declaration the database vouches for, as zeta did), never from the entity; let a type name an applet, so an override is a registration, not an edit to every view. Questions: (a) what a document declares about itself (types, labels, which paths are writable, which the permit already says); (b) whether the permit table and the page come from the same declaration; (c) where the override ladder stops, and write it down: Landfall's most powerful hooks (type templates, swapping controls, page blocks) were never documented; (d) the evidence: which screens did Landfall's users actually live in, custom or generic? Start with a story no example tells yet: reference data nobody would write a story for, e.g. 'The couple add a venue, and it is in the list' with no view written for venues.
note: 2026-09-24: added after comparing eta with Genoa/Landfall. Open, for Peter.

summary: Paging and streaming: no story yet reads past the first page or receives a result over time
detail: Landfall (2013) had it from the start: genoa_list(model, criteria, offset, limit, summary, order_by) answered {items, count, summary}; table_limit 24 on a desktop, 10 on a phone, -1 for all; a pagination template; per-collection limits; totals (sum, avg) worked out over the whole filtered set, not the page. eta today: chat reads the latest 50 messages (room.ts, LIMIT) and nothing reaches older ones; bento's find dims and counts, never hides, so a filter doesn't reduce what is sent; every write redraws each reader's whole page on the server and diffs it against the page last sent, which server.ts keeps per connection, so cost grows with page size times readers. concept found whole-document transport breaks at ~5k records, and concept/scale.md has real sizes (85k allocations, 40k areas). Two things, related: PAGING, a window onto a collection, and STREAMING, rows arriving over time (a feed, a long result from a Bun `$` callout or an outside queue written back as facts, a slow first page). Much of the machinery exists: doc names are data, and compartment.ts already expects 'one whose name is criteria (this month's appointments, last month's)'; the address (`path?what=which`) could carry the window, so the back button pages; parts.ts already sends rows added to or removed from a list as `after`/`before`/`remove`, which is the wire shape of streaming. Questions: (a) the window in the document's name (`room:general?before=812`) or in the tray's address; (b) who is told: a write lands on `room:general`, and reading() records the name the page read, so a window's readers are told only if the window reads its base document too, or the kernel learns that one name belongs to a family of names; (c) keyset (before=id) or offset: an offset moves under a concurrent insert (room.ts line 31 uses LIMIT 1 OFFSET), a keyset does not; (d) totals and counts over the whole set are a read of their own, as the wedding's counts already are; (e) the harness: a cast whose pages are windows, and `seen`/`unseen` for someone who has scrolled away. Stories to start from: 'Ada scrolls back past the first fifty messages and reads what Bob said yesterday'; 'Bob speaks while Ada is reading old messages, and her place does not move'.
note: 2026-09-24: added after comparing eta with Genoa/Landfall. Distributed work itself is out of scope (Bun `$` or a queue, not eta or delta); only how its result arrives belongs here. Open, for Peter.

summary: Stale writes: two people changing one value, and the last write silently wins
detail: Genoa (2013) had optimistic locking: a `Versioned` model carried `_version_`, a save sent the version it was based on, and `from_pairs` raised 'Version mismatch' on a stale one (Genoa/src/genoa/access/versioned.py). An eta write carries no base version, and PatchOp is add, replace and remove only, so two people replacing one path both land, in arrival order, and the first never learns it was overwritten. `data-write-on="input"` (debounced, K3) makes it likelier: a field is written while someone else reads it. RFC 6902 already has the guard: a `test` op, which fails the whole patch unless the value at the path is what the writer saw; eta's three verbs stay three, and `test` is a condition, not a change. Alternatives: the version the page was drawn at, sent with the write and checked against the document's version (coarser: any write to the document refuses, not just one to the same path). Questions: (a) `test` per path or version per document; (b) what the refused writer sees (see n5); (c) whether undo and redo, which apply a recorded inverse, carry a test of their own, since walking back over someone else's later write is the same problem; (d) the harness needs two members writing one path. Story: 'Ann and Bob both change the notional; Bob's is refused, and he sees Ann's.'
note: 2026-09-24: from the Genoa/Landfall comparison. Open, for Peter.

summary: A refused write says nothing: the page comes back and the change is gone, with no reason
detail: Genoa (2013) sent the reason back: `_validate_()` returned errors, genoa_save raised ValidationException(errors), Application.request answered `error=ex.errors`, and Landfall's form showed them against the fields. eta: server.ts runs permit() for each op, then write(); a write that applies nothing (refused by permit, a patch() that finds nothing to change, a document the connection does not see) falls through to `if (!wrote) pushRender(ws)`, which sends the page whole. The person's edit vanishes, and neither permit() (a boolean) nor write() (a WriteResult) has anywhere to say why. The stories check refusals (`cannot`), but only that nothing changed, not that the person was told. In eta's terms the reason is state, so it belongs in a document, and the tray (the session's own document) is the one already seen only by its own session: a refused write records the reason there, and the page draws it. Questions: (a) whether permit returns a reason instead of false, or refusal is a separate path; (b) whether a reason is per path (next to the field, as Landfall did) or per write; (c) when it clears: on the next write, or when the person leaves the page; (d) whether the reason goes on the ledger (no: the ledger records what happened, and a refusal did not); (e) the harness: `cannot` could assert what the refused person is shown. Story: 'Bob gives a negative quantity, is refused, and is told why next to the field.'
note: 2026-09-24: from the Genoa/Landfall comparison. Pairs with n4, whose refused writer needs this. Open, for Peter. 2026-09-24 (round 2): a refusal now ends a form's wait and hands back what was sent (b198341), and a malformed or failing write is answered with the page too (73e2b3f); the reason is still not said.

summary: Whose history: the ledger records per document, so a row written through two documents has its history split
detail: Genoa (2013) audited per row: Audit held the entity's type and primary key, before-values, what changed and who, for every create, update, delete and many-to-many add or remove, whichever screen made the change, and get_audit_trail(obj) answered 'what happened to this deal'. eta's ledger is keyed by document (`<docType>:<docId>`), with ops as JSON Pointer paths into that document. When one row can be written through two documents, its history is split: in the wedding, gift_claims rows are inserted by both board.ts (the couple) and household.ts (a household), so one claim's history is under `board:…` and `household:…`, at different paths. An auditor, or 'why is the casserole the Okafors'?', asks about the thing, not the screen. Options: (a) a rule: every row has exactly one owning document, and other documents only read it (documents-history.md's open question 5, 'every field has exactly one writing actor', said again for rows), which the harness or a test could check; (b) a ledger index by entity: patch() reports the rows it touched alongside the ops, so history can be asked by row; (c) accept it and let history be asked across documents by a join the example writes. It also affects n1: reading a row as it stood on a date needs to know where its history is. Story: 'The couple ask who claimed the casserole and when, and see the Okafors' claim and Ben's withdrawn one.'
note: 2026-09-24: from the Genoa/Landfall comparison. Related to n1. Open, for Peter.

summary: The README's cost numbers are written by hand, and go stale
detail: At 0.46.0 the README's 'Why eta' said 'a chat message is 425 bytes to each other member, a price tick 104' while its Cost section said 804 B and 111 B; on delta a run gives 1,111 B and 186 B, which the README's 'What a write costs' now says, copied by hand (24 Sep). The 17 Sep review already found story counts and byte tables stale ('Measured, not claimed: Stale'). Landfall (2013) is the long version of the same drift: its docs disagreed with its code in about ten places (panels.rst defaults, key names, a merge-conflict marker left in, examples showing the wrong key; see ~/Workshop/archive/post-peleton/overview.md), and its most powerful hooks were never written down. The README already says of story counts 'a number in a README goes stale and a run does not'. Do the same for bytes: the measure scripts write the tables (or a check fails when the README's numbers differ from a run), and prose quotes no number the tables don't.

summary: Pluggable identity: the database today, OAuth2 or LDAP tomorrow, behind one seam at /ws
detail: Authorization is already pluggable (permit, own, resolveDoc and reading(), Example.active); authentication is not. server.ts's `/ws` takes the `session_id` cookie or makes a random UUID and upgrades; ConnectionData is `{ sessionId }`; an example cannot refuse an upgrade or attach a verified identity, and cannot replace /ws ('a kernel route of the same path wins'). Every connection is an anonymous visit, and logging in is a write to the session document that the example's compartment judges: the wedding checks an invitation code (`replace /code`, kindOf) against its tables; chat's `/name` is no authentication at all. That is the database as the identity provider, done per example. It is fine for a shared code and wrong for a password: a password sent as a patch sits in the client's `window.eta.inspect().lastSent` and op log and may be echoed to the session's tabs. Genoa (2013) had the same split: AccessControl._login_ against the Person table, then Robert Betts's LDAPMixin overriding _login_ with an LDAP bind (Genoa/src/genoa/access/ldap_mixin.py): one method, swapped. The shape for eta: a provider is (1) HTTP routes on Example.routes (db or LDAP: POST /login with credentials; OAuth2: GET /login redirecting with state and PKCE, GET /callback exchanging the code with fetch and verifying the id_token), and (2) what they all end with: a verified identity and roles, a FRESH session_id cookie (never the pre-login one: session fixation), and the session document written server-side through the example's own document patch() and notify(), with its identity and role paths refused over the wire by permit(). The kernel's one new seam: an optional `Example.identify(req)` called at /ws before the upgrade, returning the session id to use or a Response to refuse, so an example can require a login, accept a reverse proxy's header (SSO), or take a bearer token from the CLI (which keeps `.eta-session` today and would need to log in too). Per provider: db passwords with Bun.password (argon2/bcrypt, built in; Genoa used salted SHA-1); OAuth2 needs no dependency beyond fetch and crypto.subtle for JWKS (or `jose`, to ask about); LDAP needs a client (`ldapts`, to ask about, and a spike under Bun). Questions: (a) identity only in the session document (eta's way), or also on ConnectionData; (b) logout: clear the cookie, delete the visit, close the sockets; (c) one provider per example, or several (codes for guests, OAuth2 for the couple); (d) the harness: casts log in through the provider, or seed sessions with roles and test the provider on its own (a test directory in Docker, a fake OAuth2 issuer). Stories: 'A visitor without a login sees only the login page and cannot write'; 'Ann logs in and sees her desk'; 'Ann cannot give herself the admin role'.
note: 2026-09-24: from the Genoa/Landfall comparison and Peter: 'right now we use the db but we could use oauth2 or ldap'. Open, for Peter.

summary: Undo puts a row back as the write found it, over what anyone wrote to it since
detail: delta 0.6.0 applies a ledger entry's recorded inverse blind (sqlite.ts inverseOf: `replace /<root> <the whole row as it was>`). Two tabs of one household: A writes the note, B writes his, A undoes -> the note is the seed's; B undoes -> A's undone note is back. Repro: the first test.failing in examples/wedding/server.test.ts ('undo beside someone else'); delta alone: delta-undo-repro.ts part 1 in scratchpad/round2-eta (eta-fixer, 24 Sep). Fix is delta's: guard each inverse with what the write left (a `test`), restore only those fields, refuse on conflict. Filed to delta in round2/cross-repo.md.
note: 2026-09-24: delta's; take the .failing off when bun says it passes.

summary: An undo whose inverse no longer applies sticks the session's Undo on it for good
detail: When the inverse fails (Row not found: another tab removed the row), delta rolls the walk back and records nothing, so nextUndo returns the same entry on every press and every earlier write of that session can never be undone. Repro: the second test.failing in examples/wedding/server.test.ts; delta alone: delta-undo-repro.ts part 2 in scratchpad/round2-eta (eta-fixer, 24 Sep). Fix is delta's: record the walk as walked-with-conflict and answer the conflict. Filed in round2/cross-repo.md.

summary: Undo and redo are not asked the compartment's rules: after the deadline, Undo still changes an answer
detail: eta's walk asks only the ledger compartment (remove/add /latest) and `Example.active`; it cannot know which entry delta will walk until delta has walked it, so a rule of time or state (the wedding's deadline, a closed poll) does not hold against Undo. Repro: the third test.failing in examples/wedding/server.test.ts; deadline.ts in scratchpad/round2-eta (eta-fixer, 24 Sep). Needs a delta seam (undo/redo with `dry: true` answering the entry, or taking the id to walk), then eta asks the owner compartment, e.g. `walkable?(ws, docId, entry)`. Not `permit` again: chat's and the wedding's '…only Undo can' stories rely on undo doing what permit refuses.
note: 2026-09-24: waits on delta's seam; the eta side is small.

summary: Undo gets slower as the whole ledger grows, the ticker's facts included
detail: delta's cursor CTE recurses on `undoes` and NOT INs the whole table; its indexes are (doc, version) and (cursor). 20 rows: 0.09 ms per nextUndo; +400k fact rows (about 2.3 days of the ticker's feed): 102 ms, on the one thread every event waits on; with an index on undoes: 10 ms. Repro: ledger-scale.ts in scratchpad/round2-eta (eta-fixer, 24 Sep). delta's to fix (an index, and a query that starts from this cursor's tips). The ticker's ledger also grows with facts nothing reads.
note: 2026-09-24: delta's; filed in round2/cross-repo.md.

summary: eta keeps its own JSON Pointer parse and applyPatch beside delta core's
detail: delta core's splitPath takes a slashless path as root and '/' as root, and parsePath turns '007' into 7; its applyOps creates a member a replace names and does not have. eta's parsePointer throws on a slashless path (the wedding's and the ticker's permits rely on it) and the harness's applyPatch must throw when an op does not land (that is how it says an applet was sent ops that do not describe its props). Swap both for delta core's once core is strict (delta's F4 and D4), and PatchOp for DeltaOp with them (documents.ts casts between the two).
note: 2026-09-24: waits on delta core.

summary: A write carries no id, so no echo can say 'yours'
detail: A form now clears as it sends and a refusal (the page whole before the echo) hands back what was sent (b198341), so no echo resets a field. Left: a whole render that comes for another reason while a write is in flight (someone else's write turns this page into another) is taken for a refusal and puts the sent text back; and eta.inspect().lastSent.echoed matches by document name, so anyone's echo marks it. Fix: `{id?, doc, ops}` on the wire, the id echoed to its writer and a refusal answered `{type: 'refused', id, reason?}` (pairs with n5).
note: 2026-09-24: round 2 left it; M, a wire change.

summary: The 100% coverage gate covers no client code
detail: src/client/app.ts, morph.ts, form-value.ts, src/applets.ts, src/island.ts and every *-applet.ts(x) run only in the browser (Bun.WebView), bundled apart from bun test's process, so the coverage table never lists them. Round 1's F6-F8 all lived there; round 2's fixes are covered by browser tests, not by the gate. Options: a happy-dom preload for unit tests of the client (railroad's approach), or collect coverage from the WebView.
note: 2026-09-24: round 1 F12a, still true.

summary: One example per process is module state, patched around for tests
detail: The module-level `active` in server.ts, audience.ts's open sockets and byDocType, and documents.ts's active copy exist so tests in one process can run one example after another; server.stop is patched to clear them. `bun test --isolate` would give each test file its own module state and let these go (the 17 Sep review counted about 23 lines). Test files also share the in-memory database, so a file that assumes the seed can be broken by another file's writes (board.test.ts assumed three gifts until a browser test added one).
note: 2026-09-24: from the 17 Sep review, still open.

summary: A story cannot say 'a tab closes', or 'meanwhile someone else writes'
detail: Presence is told by the socket (a tab closing changes who is in a room), and undo beside another writer needs a write between a story's does and its undo; neither has a key. The first is fixed in the code (every change is told from delta's stream, so a closing tab reaches every reader; tab-close.ts in scratchpad/round2-eta (eta-fixer, 24 Sep)), the second is n9-n11. stories.md says a sixth key waits until a stories.ts needs it: 'Cy closes her tab, and Ada and Bob see her leave general' and 'Ada takes back her note, and Femi's, written after, stays' are the candidates.
note: 2026-09-24: round 1's B5 and meanwhile.

summary: Nothing in eta provisions a browser for its browser tests
detail: With Chromium the suite is green (BUN_CHROME_PATH=/opt/chromium/chrome-shim.sh bun test: 311 pass); without it, every Bun.WebView test fails to spawn Chrome. railroad's SessionStart hook stages Chromium from the @sparticuz/chromium npm tarball, but installs with npm, which eta's CLAUDE.md rules out. A Bun-only hook (bunx, or a fetch of the tarball) shared by the three repos would close it.

summary: One document named by a live session's id stops the telling of its change to everyone
detail: tellChanges echoes to each socket with wireName, which throws, loudly and on purpose, for a document keyed by a live session id that is not `own`; the throw ends that change's echo and redraws for every socket after it (caught per listener in documents.ts). A per-socket guard would keep the others told while the failure is still reported.
